chartContributions.notes: Spelled Bellinghausen on both charts. The transliteration is the chart's, not ours, and is kept as the chart gives it.
A commercial voyage compiled into an Admiralty chart, which is the point at which sealing knowledge becomes hydrographic knowledge.
The oldest voyage on both sheets, and the only one that predates the idea of an Antarctic continent as a survey target.
One of the two additions that distinguish the 1910 issue from its 1874 predecessor.

The chart dates d'Urville 1839 although the Adelie coast sighting is generally dated January 1840. A chart's own dating is evidence about the chart, and is recorded as the chart gives it rather than corrected silently.
A magnetic and pendulum survey, present on the chart for its ice observations rather than for any discovery.
The other addition, and the reason the 1910 sheet exists at all.
The last voyage on the 1874 sheet, and the survey the earlier sightings are reconciled against.

Not a voyage but a set of papers on icebergs, credited in the 1874 title and absent from the 1910 one. A compilation that cites an analysis rather than an observation is exactly the distinction between surveyed and reconciled geography, and it is the one contribution here that never went south.
The exceptional ice year, compiled alongside ordinary ones without a note that it was exceptional. That flattening is itself part of what Act VII should show.
Same dating question as d'Urville. Wilkes appears on a chart that also carries Ross, whose voyage contradicted part of what Wilkes charted.

coastline.notes: Confirmed by the Australasian expedition seventy years later, which is also why Mawson is a Act VII candidate on cartographic rather than heroic grounds.
A hundred years between the claim and any reliable confirmation date, and the confirmation date recorded here is itself approximate. That interval is the finding, not a defect in the row.

Filed as modified rather than confirmed because an ice front is not a coastline and does not stay where it was charted. A chronology that treated it as confirmed coast would be wrong in a way no later survey could correct.
No geometry: what was seen and where is the contested question, and drawing a segment would answer it. The chronology fields carry what is known, which is a claimed date and nothing confirmed.
The only segment here filed as a direct observation, and the one whose four dates are all present. It is the shape a well-evidenced coast has, and the others are measured against it.

coastline.displayName: The coast charted as Wilkes Land
coastline.notes: `first_observed_date` is deliberately empty while `first_claimed_date` is not. That gap between claiming and observing is the whole of the Wilkes problem, and a schema that forced one date would hide it.

phases.notes: Sequence 0 because it never happened. It is the intention against which every later phase is read, and it is held as a separate entity so that the plan and the experience can never be merged into one route.

phases.displayName: South Georgia into the Weddell Sea
phases.notes: The only phase in which the ship goes where it is steered.
The hinge of the act. Recorded as 19 January; sources seen during compilation also give 18 January, and that disagreement is logged as ant-gap-besetment-date rather than resolved by choosing.
Nine months in which the ship's position changes continuously and its crew steer nothing. The `under_own_power` field exists for this row: a drift must never read as a voyage.
Abandonment and sinking are twenty-five days apart and are two events, not one.
The people continue to move geographically after the ship is gone, which is the cleanest statement of the act's question.
A second navigation problem with different constraints: few sights, a moving platform and no margin for a longitude error.
Included because it is navigation without a chart, which is the last variation the act has to offer.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Whether an ice front counts as a sighting of land
priorityClaims.notes: The strongest case if an ice front observed from close inshore counts, and no case at all if the definition requires rock. That is a definitional question, not an evidential one, and the row records which definition it answers rather than whether it wins.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Whether what was seen was the mainland peninsula or islands off it
priorityClaims.notes: Three days after Bellingshausen and against a different definition, which is why comparing the two dates settles nothing on its own.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Overlap in time and place with the United States squadron
priorityClaims.notes: Three expeditions on overlapping coast in one season is the best case Act V has, and the essay currently has one of the three charts located.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: A sealing log as the record, and a date ten months later than the other two
priorityClaims.notes: The weakest of the three on date alone, and the one whose evidence is a commercial document rather than a naval one. Both facts are about the archive, not about what was seen.

priorityClaims.assertedBy: Argument from the incentives of the trade
priorityClaims.notes: Recorded as a row with no date and no observation, which is the honest shape of an argument from silence. It exists so the contest cannot be presented as a closed field of three.

priorityClaims.contestedBy: Ross sailing across positions charted as land
priorityClaims.notes: A claim to continental extent rather than to a first sighting, which is a different contest and is filed as one. Parts of it survived and parts did not.

records.notes: The furthest south of the second voyage, commonly given as 71 degrees 10 minutes south, 106 degrees 54 minutes west. Recorded from the general literature and not yet checked against Beaglehole, which is why it stays raw.
records.title: Southern limit reached by Resolution, 30 January 1774

records.notes: A non-spatial evidence record. The plate has not been seen, so the record exists to hold the question rather than to answer it, and carries no geometry precisely because inventing one would be the error Act III is about.
records.title: Coronelli's southern polar region, as treated in 1693

records.notes: The one pilot record whose identity is established from a catalogue record read directly, which is why it is the only row at normalized. Its later_status is modified rather than confirmed because the sheet is itself a reissue of an 1874 compilation.
records.title: Cumulative southern ice chart, 1910 issue

records.notes: A latitude envelope standing for the region within which the conjectured continent was drawn. It is deliberately not a coastline: no map in the register has been examined, so there is nothing to digitise, and drawing a plausible outline would manufacture the very false precision the essay is about.
records.title: Terra Australis, schematic envelope (not a digitised coastline)

records.laterEvidence: Reported to have been searched for without result and eventually removed from charts. No authority for the removal is held here.
records.notes: A sub-Antarctic phantom rather than a continental one, kept because it is the clearest case of the pattern the reusable methodology is for: report, repetition, search, removal. Filed as unresolved rather than disproved: the removal is reported but no authority for it is held, and the validator refuses a disproof that cannot name what disproved it. Ramsay is a popular survey and the audit has already ruled that it may not carry an individual case.
records.title: Dougherty Island
records.whatWasReported: An island reported in the far South Pacific, with a described position, subsequently repeated on charts and searched for by later vessels.
records.whyPlausible: A single reported position in an ocean nobody crossed often, in an era when a chart had no way to record that a feature rested on one unconfirmed report.

records.laterEvidence: Reported to have been searched for without result and eventually removed from charts. No authority for the removal is held here.
records.notes: The same pattern as Dougherty and worth holding beside it, because two independent phantoms in the same waters say something about the waters rather than about the observers. Filed as unresolved rather than disproved: the removal is reported but no authority for it is held, and the validator refuses a disproof that cannot name what disproved it.
records.title: Emerald Island
records.whatWasReported: An island reported south of New Zealand and carried on charts for over a century.
records.whyPlausible: The southern ocean between Australasia and the ice was crossed rarely and charted from scattered reports, so a single sighting had little against it.

records.laterEvidence: Later voyages, including the Endurance drift across much of the same water, found open sea and pack where the coast was placed.
records.notes: The programme's strongest ghost case after Wilkes, and the one that connects Act VI directly to Act VIII: Endurance drifted through the water Morrell had charted as land. Morrell's reliability is separately disputed in the literature, which is a question about the man and not about the feature, and the two are kept apart. No cause is attributed.
records.title: New South Greenland
records.whatWasReported: An extensive coast reported in the Weddell Sea, running south from around 62 degrees south, described with landmarks and soundings.
records.whyPlausible: Morrell was sailing in the same exceptional ice year that let Weddell reach an extraordinary latitude, in a sea that was demonstrably open that season and closed in most others. A coast reported from there in 1823 was not absurd on its face.

records.laterEvidence: Later parties working over the same ground did not find a range as charted.
records.notes: Included because the claimant is the most reliable observer in the dataset. A ghost feature attributable to a careless witness teaches nothing; one attributable to Ross is the whole argument of Act VI. The plausibility note stops short of naming refraction as the cause, because no source is held for that.
records.title: The Parry Mountains
records.whatWasReported: A range reported to the south of the Ross Sea coast and named after Ross's former commander.
records.whyPlausible: Ross was an experienced observer working in clear polar air, where distance and elevation are notoriously hard to judge and where a far snowfield can read as a nearer range.

records.laterEvidence: Later vessels sailed across positions charted as land.
records.notes: Deliberately carries no geometry. Which segment, at what position, on which sheet is unknown (ant-gap-wilkes-sheets), and drawing a line for a disproof we cannot locate would repeat the original error in our own voice. current_scholarly_status stays unresolved because much of Wilkes's coast was correct.
records.title: Coast charted by Wilkes and later sailed through (segment to be identified)
records.whatWasReported: Continuous southern coast observed and charted over an extended run of longitude.
records.whyPlausible: A long coast seen repeatedly over many days from a squadron of ships, in conditions where distant ice and distant land are hard to tell apart.

records.notes: Filed as reported_not_observed rather than direct_observation on purpose: what was seen, and whether it counts as a sighting of the mainland, is the disputed question the terminology table exists to keep open. The position is approximate and taken from the general literature.
records.title: Reported sighting of an ice front, Vostok and Mirny

records.notes: Named on both cumulative ice charts for the 1839 season. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Islands sighted, later named the Balleny Islands

records.notes: A commercial voyage producing coast. Position approximate to the region rather than to a landfall. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Land sighted and named Enderby Land

records.notes: One of the three 1820 claims. Position approximate. Filed as a report rather than an observation because what was seen, and whether it was the mainland or an island of the peninsula group, is the argument. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Land sighted from Williams, named Trinity Land

records.notes: Recorded from the general literature. The figure is stable across accounts but has not been read in the edition, so it stays raw.
records.title: Farthest south, Resolution

records.notes: One of three expeditions on overlapping coast in the same weeks. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Coast sighted and named Terre Adelie

records.notes: Approximate. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: The boats reach Elephant Island

records.notes: Approximate, and separate from the sinking a month later. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Endurance abandoned

records.notes: Approximate, recorded from the general literature and unverified. Whether the position was fixed or reckoned is unknown until the navigational records are found.
records.title: Endurance beset in the pack

records.notes: The last position before the pack. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Endurance leaves South Georgia

records.notes: The figure usually given as 68 degrees 39 minutes 30 seconds south, 52 degrees 26 minutes 30 seconds west. It is recorded at the precision the literature reports and at low confidence, because the whole point of the Coda is that this coordinate is a calculated result with an error nobody here has yet established.
records.title: Position recorded for the loss of Endurance

records.notes: The start of the second navigation problem, and the one Worsley wrote a whole book about. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: James Caird leaves Elephant Island

records.notes: Approximate. The accuracy of the passage that ended here is the claim the ledger refuses to quantify without a technical source. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: The James Caird makes South Georgia

records.notes: The American claim, resting on a sealing log. Recorded to the month because the day is not established here. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Land sighted from Hero

records.notes: Approximate. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Farthest south reached by Erebus and Terror

records.notes: The first record in the dataset filed as a direct observation of coast, because Ross's survey followed it rather than passing once. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Coast sighted and named Victoria Land

records.notes: An exceptional open-water penetration in an exceptional ice year, which later voyages could not repeat. The date and position are approximate. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Farthest south reached by Jane

records.notes: Recorded to the month deliberately: the exact days are part of the priority dispute with d'Urville, and settling them here would settle the dispute by data entry. Recorded from the general literature during compilation and not yet checked against an edition, so the row stays raw.
records.title: Land reported from the United States squadron

records.notes: Four points standing for a two-year track. It is a sample that proves the schema carries a line, not a route anyone may measure. The real track is compiled at ANT-5 from the journals.
records.title: Resolution in the high southern latitudes, 1773-1774 (sample)

records.notes: The last stretch under the ship's own power, held apart from the drift that follows it so that the moment the vessel stops navigating is a change in the data and not only in the prose.
records.title: Endurance from South Georgia into the Weddell Sea (sample)

records.notes: Two endpoints joined by a straight line, which the drift certainly was not. Present only to prove the schema can hold a drift distinct from a planned route; ANT-9 replaces it with dated positions.
records.title: Endurance in the ice, besetment to loss (two-point sample)

records.notes: A planned route is an intention, not an observation, and this drawing of it is ours. It is filed as editorial_interpolation so that no part of the pipeline can mistake it for evidence, which is the distinction Act VIII turns on.
records.title: Planned trans-Antarctic crossing, as announced

records.notes: Three points for a sixteen-day passage. The middle point is ours entirely, which is why the whole track is filed as interpolation: Worsley's observed fixes are the record, and a smooth line between endpoints is the opposite of what this act is about. ANT-10 replaces it with the fixes.
records.title: James Caird, Elephant Island to South Georgia (endpoint sample)
